```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.2)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(sf)
  library(tmap)
  library(VancouvR)
})
options(pillar.sigfig = 7)
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")
```

## bca knows where each home is, but not what is near it

```{r}
#| label: bca-lonlat
bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver") |>
  select(neigh_label, price, lon, lat) |>
  head(3)
```

To R, `lon` and `lat` are just numbers. It cannot yet tell which local area a sale is in, how far it is from SkyTrain, or whether it is in the floodplain.

The **sf** (simple features) package turns coordinates into points that R can measure and match against areas.

::: {.notes}
- The slides print 7 significant digits (`options(pillar.sigfig = 7)` in the hidden setup chunk). With the default of 3, `lon` prints as `-123.`, which hides that the column holds coordinates.
:::

## The City of Vancouver publishes spatial data

```{r}
#| label: local-areas
local_areas <- get_cov_data("local-area-boundary")
```

`get_cov_data()` from **VancouvR** downloads a dataset from [City of Vancouver Open Data](https://opendata.vancouver.ca/). The ID is the end of the dataset's web address. No API key is needed.

::: {.small}
| ID | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `local-area-boundary` | The 22 local areas |
| `rapid-transit-stations`, `rapid-transit-lines` | SkyTrain stations and lines |
| `zoning-districts-and-labels` | Zoning districts |
| `designated-floodplain` | Areas at risk of flooding |
| `issued-building-permits` | Building permits, with project values |
| `non-market-housing` | Social and co-op housing projects |
:::

## An sf object is a tibble with a geometry column

```{r}
#| label: print-sf
head(local_areas, 3)
```

Each row is one local area. `geometry` holds its boundary: the corners of a polygon, in degrees (°).

## tm_shape() starts a map

```{r}
#| label: map-areas
tm_shape(local_areas) +
  tm_polygons()
```

**tmap** draws sf objects. `tm_shape()` names the data; `tm_polygons()` draws it. Deck 13 covers tmap in full.

## Points, lines, and polygons stack as layers

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: layers
#| eval: false
stations <-
  get_cov_data("rapid-transit-stations")
transit_lines <-
  get_cov_data("rapid-transit-lines")

tm_shape(local_areas) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95") +
  tm_shape(transit_lines) +
  tm_lines(col = "steelblue", lwd = 2) +
  tm_shape(stations) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.4)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r}
#| label: layers-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
stations <- get_cov_data("rapid-transit-stations")
transit_lines <- get_cov_data("rapid-transit-lines")

tm_shape(local_areas) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey95") +
  tm_shape(transit_lines) + tm_lines(col = "steelblue", lwd = 2) +
  tm_shape(stations) + tm_dots(size = 0.4)
```
:::
::::

Each `tm_shape()` starts a layer, and later layers draw on top, as in ggplot. The first layer sets the map's extent, so the Expo Line stops at the city boundary.

## In tmap, the value decides: mapping or setting

```{r}
#| label: skytrain-areas
areas <- local_areas |>
  mutate(skytrain = name %in% stations$geo_local_area)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: fill-setting
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
tm_shape(areas) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "blue")
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: fill-mapping
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
tm_shape(areas) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "skytrain")
```
:::
::::

tmap has no `aes()`. A column name, such as `"skytrain"`, is mapped and gets a legend. Any other value, such as `"blue"`, is a setting. A misspelled column name stops with an error.

::: {.notes}
- In ggplot, *where* you write it decides: inside or outside `aes()` (deck 06). In tmap, *what* you write decides. Deck 06's trap, `aes(colour = "blue")` turning a constant into a legend, cannot happen in tmap.
- If the data had a column named `blue`, `fill = "blue"` would map that column: a column name wins over a colour.
- The typo error reads: "Visual values used for the variable "fill" are incorrect. Variable should a data variable name or a single color."
- On the last slide, `fill = "grey95"`, `col = "steelblue"`, `lwd = 2`, and `size = 0.4` are all settings.
:::

## dplyr verbs keep the geometry

```{r}
#| label: sticky
stations |> filter(geo_local_area == "Oakridge") |> select(station)
```

We kept only `station`, but `geometry` came along: it is **sticky**.

## st_drop_geometry() returns a plain tibble

```{r}
#| label: drop
stations |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(geo_local_area, sort = TRUE) |> head(3)
```

Drop the geometry when you only need a table: counts and summaries run faster, and the output is shorter.

## st_read() reads spatial files

Other portals let you download files instead.

- **GeoJSON**: one file, such as `data/Park_Inventory.geojson`.
- **Shapefile**: several files with one name (`.shp`, `.shx`, `.dbf`, `.prj`, …). Keep them together and read the `.shp`.

```{r}
#| label: st-read
parks <- st_read("data/Park_Inventory.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
parks_shp <- st_read("data/Park_Inventory/Park_Inventory.shp", quiet = TRUE)
c(geojson = nrow(parks), shapefile = nrow(parks_shp))
```

Both hold Burnaby's parks, from [Burnaby Open Data](https://data.burnaby.ca/).

## st_as_sf() turns longitude and latitude into points

```{r}
#| label: sales
sales <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2025,
         !is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  select(folioid, act_use_cat, price, floorarea, lon, lat) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
nrow(sales)
```

- `coords`: the x column first (longitude), then y (latitude).
- `crs = 4326`: the numbers are degrees of longitude and latitude.
- `st_as_sf()` stops at a missing coordinate, so drop those rows first.

## Map new points before you use them

```{r}
#| label: map-sales
tm_shape(local_areas) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey95") +
  tm_shape(sales) + tm_dots(fill = "act_use_cat", size = 0.1)
```

## Quick check: what does this do?

```{r}
#| label: quiz-swap
#| eval: false
swapped <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2025,
         !is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lat", "lon"), crs = 4326)
```

**A.** Stops with an error  **B.** Puts the points in the wrong place

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: quiz-swap-answer
#| echo: false
swapped <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2025,
         !is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lat", "lon"), crs = 4326)
st_bbox(swapped) |> round(1)
```

**B.** Latitude is now −123, which cannot exist: latitudes run from −90 to 90. R made the points anyway. Map new points before you use them.
:::

## A coordinate reference system gives the numbers meaning

::: {.small}
| EPSG code | Name | Units | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4326 | WGS 84 | degrees | Longitude and latitude: `bca`, City open data, GPS |
| 26910 | NAD83 / UTM zone 10N | metres | Distances, buffers, and areas in BC |
| 3347 | Statistics Canada Lambert | metres | Maps of all of Canada |
:::

```{r}
#| label: crs
st_crs(stations)$epsg
```

The City's data, like `bca`, use EPSG 4326.

## st_transform() changes the numbers, not the places

```{r}
#| label: transform
st_bbox(stations) |> round(3)
stations |> st_transform(26910) |> st_bbox() |> round()
```

```{r}
#| label: span
#| include: false
bb_m <- st_bbox(st_transform(stations, 26910))
span_km <- round(c(x = bb_m[["xmax"]] - bb_m[["xmin"]], y = bb_m[["ymax"]] - bb_m[["ymin"]]) / 1000, 1)
```

`st_bbox()` gives the smallest box around the data. In metres, the stations span `r span_km[["x"]]` km east to west and `r span_km[["y"]]` km north to south.

## Check the coordinates, not only the guide

```{r}
#| label: crimes
vpd_file <- file.path("data", "crimedata_csv_AllNeighbourhoods_2026",
                      "crimedata_csv_AllNeighbourhoods_2026.csv")
crimes <- read_csv(vpd_file)
crimes |> select(TYPE, X, Y) |> head(3)
```

The Vancouver Police Department's guide says the coordinates are in "latitude and longitude" on one page and in "UTM Zone 10" on another. An `X` of 492,734 cannot be a longitude: these are metres.

## Declare the CRS the data use

```{r}
#| label: crimes-sf
crimes_sf <- crimes |>
  filter(X != 0) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = 26910)
crimes_sf |> st_transform(4326) |> st_bbox() |> round(3)
```

With `crs = 4326`, the same code runs without an error, and every crime gets an impossible longitude of about 490,000.

::: {.warning}
`X` is 0 when VPD withholds the location. In this file, that is every offence against a person and the one homicide: `r sum(crimes$X == 0)` crimes. A map of the remaining points shows no violent crime at all.
:::

## st_join() attaches the area each point falls in

```{r}
#| label: join
sales_area <- st_join(sales, local_areas)
c(before = nrow(sales), after = nrow(sales_area))

sales_area |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(name, sort = TRUE) |> head(4)
```

Each sale gets the `name` of its local area. Both layers must use the same CRS.

## Join the other way to map each area

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: by-area
#| eval: false
strata <- sales |>
  filter(act_use_cat == "Strata Res")

strata_by_area <-
  st_join(local_areas, strata) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(sales = n(),
            median_price = median(price))

tm_shape(strata_by_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "median_price")
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r}
#| label: by-area-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
strata <- sales |> filter(act_use_cat == "Strata Res")

strata_by_area <- st_join(local_areas, strata) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(sales = n(), median_price = median(price))

tm_shape(strata_by_area) + tm_polygons(fill = "median_price")
```
:::
::::

Each area matches many sales. `summarise()` merges each area's rows back into one polygon.

::: {.notes}
- `st_join(local_areas, strata)` keeps an area with no strata sale as one row with `NA` columns, so `n()` would report 1 sale there. In 2025 every area has at least `r min(strata_by_area$sales)` strata sales. If that could happen, count `sum(!is.na(price))` instead.
- Strata only, because the mix of houses and strata differs by area (deck 05).
:::

## Same name, different boundaries

```{r}
#| label: kerr-data
#| include: false
kerr17 <- bca |>
  filter(neigh_label == "Kerrisdale", year(sale_date) == 2017, !is.na(lon)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_join(local_areas)
kerr_n <- kerr17 |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(name, sort = TRUE)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: kerr
#| eval: false
kerr17 <- bca |>
  filter(neigh_label == "Kerrisdale",
         year(sale_date) == 2017, !is.na(lon)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_join(local_areas)

kerr17 |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(name, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: kerr-count
#| echo: false
kerr_n
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
```{r}
#| label: kerr-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
tm_shape(local_areas |> filter(name %in% kerr_n$name)) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95") + tm_text("name", size = 0.7) +
  tm_shape(kerr17) + tm_dots(fill = "name", size = 0.3, fill.legend = tm_legend_hide())
```
:::
::::

Deck 06's `kerr17` uses BC Assessment's Kerrisdale. Only `r kerr_n$n[kerr_n$name == "Kerrisdale"]` of its `r nrow(kerr17)` sales are in the City's Kerrisdale. Match areas by location, not by name.

## Measure distance in metres

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: distance
sales_m <- st_transform(sales, 26910)
stations_m <- st_transform(stations, 26910)

nearest <- st_nearest_feature(sales_m, stations_m)
dist <- st_distance(sales_m, stations_m[nearest, ], by_element = TRUE)

sales_m <- sales_m |>
  mutate(station = stations_m$station[nearest], dist_m = as.numeric(dist))
sales_m |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(price, station, dist_m) |> head(3)
```
:::

`st_nearest_feature()` finds the row of the closest station; `st_distance()` measures the distance to it. In EPSG 26910, the answer is in metres.

::: {.notes}
- With longitude and latitude, sf also measures in metres on a sphere (the s2 engine), but buffers are approximate: a 500 m buffer came out 1.5% too large in area.
- AI code often calls `sf_use_s2(FALSE)` to silence a geometry error. Then `st_buffer(x, 500)` on longitude and latitude draws circles 500 degrees wide. Transforming to metres first avoids both problems.
:::

## Strata prices and distance to SkyTrain

```{r}
#| label: dist-plot
#| fig-height: 3.4
strata_m <- sales_m |> filter(act_use_cat == "Strata Res", !is.na(floorarea))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(dist_m, price / floorarea), alpha = 0.2, data = strata_m)
```

```{r}
#| label: ppsf
#| include: false
ppsf <- strata_m |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(near = dist_m <= 500) |>
  summarise(median = median(price / floorarea))
ppsf_near <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)(ppsf$median[ppsf$near])
ppsf_far <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)(ppsf$median[!ppsf$near])
```

Median price per square foot: `r ppsf_near` within 500 m of a station, `r ppsf_far` farther away. A vertical stripe is many sales at one distance, such as units in one building.

::: {.notes}
- Stations cluster Downtown and along a few corridors, so near and far sales differ in more than distance: age, size, views, and neighbourhood. Deck 18 asks why a raw comparison like this can mislead, and deck 17's fixed effects compare like with like.
:::

## A buffer covers everything within a distance

```{r}
#| label: buffer
#| fig-height: 3.8
buffers <- st_buffer(stations_m, 500)

tm_shape(local_areas) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey95") +
  tm_shape(buffers) + tm_polygons(fill = "steelblue", fill_alpha = 0.4)
```

`st_buffer(500)` draws a 500-unit circle around each station. In EPSG 26910, that is 500 metres.

## Overlapping buffers duplicate rows

```{r}
#| label: dup
sales_near <- st_join(sales_m, buffers)
c(before = nrow(sales_m), after = nrow(sales_near))
```

::: {.warning}
A sale within 500 m of two stations matches both, so it appears twice. Counts per station are right, but totals and averages across sales count those sales twice.
:::

::: {.key-point}
After every spatial join, compare the row counts and map the result.
:::

## Practice: sales in the floodplain

How many 2025 sales in the City of Vancouver were of homes in the designated floodplain?

1. Download `designated-floodplain` with `get_cov_data()`.
2. Join `sales` to it, keeping only the sales inside: `st_join(sales, floodplain, left = FALSE)`.
3. Check the row count. Does each sale appear once?
4. Map the floodplain and the sales in it.

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: flood
floodplain <- get_cov_data("designated-floodplain")

in_flood <- st_join(sales, floodplain, left = FALSE)
nrow(in_flood)
in_flood |> st_drop_geometry() |> count(name)

nrow(st_filter(sales, floodplain))
```
:::

The floodplain layers overlap, so `r nrow(in_flood) - nrow(st_filter(sales, floodplain))` sales matched two of them. `st_filter()` keeps each sale once: `r nrow(st_filter(sales, floodplain))` sales.

## Answer: the map

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: flood-map
#| fig-height: 4.2
tm_shape(local_areas) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey95") +
  tm_shape(floodplain) + tm_polygons(fill = "steelblue", fill_alpha = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(st_filter(sales, floodplain)) + tm_dots(size = 0.15)
```

## What to know from this deck

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%"}
**Know**<br>*Write it without help*

::: {.small}
- `st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)`
- `st_join()`, then compare row counts
- `st_drop_geometry()`
- `tm_shape()` + `tm_polygons()`, `tm_dots()`; a column name in `fill =` maps, a colour sets
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
**Recognize**<br>*Say what the line does*

::: {.small}
- `get_cov_data("id")`, `st_read()`
- `st_crs()`, `st_transform(26910)`
- `st_buffer()`, `st_distance()`, `st_nearest_feature()`
- `st_filter()`: keep the points inside, once each
:::
:::

::: {.column width="24%"}
**Look up**<br>*When you meet it*

::: {.small}
- EPSG codes
- `tm_lines()`, `fill_alpha`
- `left = FALSE`
- `by_element = TRUE`
:::
:::
::::

::: {.key-point}
Check new points on a map, and check the row count after every spatial join.
:::
